# DRAFT FOR PRESIDENT & CEO SIGN-OFF (due Fri 23 Oct 2026) - not for transmission

**AMERICAN COMPUTE & INNOVATION ALLIANCE**
Washington, D.C.

Oct. 29, 2026

Rep. Jay Obernolte
Rep. Lori Trahan
Committee on Energy and Commerce
U.S. House of Representatives
Washington, D.C. 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

**Re: Comments of the American Compute & Innovation Alliance on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft**

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

The American Compute & Innovation Alliance thanks you for releasing the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act as a discussion draft and for keeping the comment record open. ACIA is a Washington-based coalition of roughly 140 members: AI developers, cloud and data center operators, chip startups and venture firms. Our members build the models, chips and data centers that will determine whether the United States leads the world in artificial intelligence.

We write with one clear message. This draft is the first bipartisan text that would give the country one national standard for frontier AI development instead of a 50-state patchwork. That is the single most pro-innovation thing Congress can do this year. We support the architecture. We ask for five targeted changes before introduction.

In our March 2025 comment to the Office of Science and Technology Policy on the AI Action Plan, ACIA urged the federal government to preempt the patchwork, unlock energy and compute, and keep standards voluntary and industry-led. The draft takes each of those ideas seriously, and we want to help you get it right.

## 1. The patchwork is the problem, and the costs are real

State legislatures have enacted roughly 150 AI laws this year alone, across 36 states. Three of them regulate frontier model development directly: California's SB 53, in effect since Jan. 1, 2026; New York's RAISE Act, as amended, effective Jan. 1, 2027; and Illinois' SB 315, signed July 6 and effective Jan. 1, 2028. They use different definitions, different reporting clocks and different audit rules. Illinois, unlike the other two, mandates third-party audits.

Our August 2026 member survey, reported here in aggregate, quantifies what that means:

- Sixty-one percent of responding members cite conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem.
- Developers running SB 53 and RAISE in parallel report a median of 6.5 full-time employees devoted to compliance.
- Thirty-four percent of our startup members delayed a product launch in California or New York in the past 12 months because of state AI rules.
- Standing up an incident-reporting function costs a median of $310,000 before a company files a single report, and maintaining a published frontier safety framework costs larger developers a median of $1.4 million a year.

Compliance costs fall hardest on startups, even though these laws are written for the largest laboratories. That is backwards. The administration reached the same conclusion in its Dec. 11, 2025 executive order on a national AI policy framework and in the March 20, 2026 White House legislative recommendations, which ask Congress to preempt state laws that impose undue burdens and to keep states out of AI model development.

## 2. Section 121 preemption: we support it. Make it durable.

ACIA supports the draft's preemption of state laws that specifically regulate the development of AI models. The draft draws the right lines: state law on use, deployment and post-deployment harms is preserved, as are laws of general applicability and common-law remedies. Consumers, workers and state attorneys general keep their tools. What goes away is the duplication that comes from three states writing three different sets of pre-deployment rules for the same model.

Our ask is about duration, not scope. A three-year sunset is a compliance cliff. No compliance officer in our membership will dismantle a state-law program that may come back into force in year four, which means the cost relief the sponsors intend never materializes. We ask that Section 121 be made permanent. At minimum, extend it on a schedule that puts a clean, enacted federal standard in place before any sunset, with a Government Accountability Office review of the federal regime before the lapse date.

We also ask that preemption reach the specific development obligations the bill federalizes in Sections 111 and 112. A developer that complies with the federal standard should not also be answering to a state scheme covering the same conduct.

## 3. Section 111 incident reporting: we oppose it as drafted

ACIA does not oppose incident reporting. We oppose this version of it, and we ask for four changes.

**Narrow the definition.** Section 101(7) defines a critical safety incident to include "a failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures." Read literally, that captures every imperfect safeguard, with no harm shown. Compare California: under SB 53, unauthorized access to model weights is reportable when it "results in death or bodily injury," and loss of control likewise requires death or bodily injury. The draft strips those harm qualifiers out. It also drops the "single incident" limiter that California attaches to catastrophic risk. Please restore a harm or concrete-incident element, and keep federal obligations anchored to demonstrated harms rather than to speculative scenarios that no one can measure.

**Hold the 15-day clock.** The draft requires a report to the CAISI director within 15 days of discovery, which matches California, with a 24-hour disclosure to law enforcement where there is an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury. That is a workable, light-touch standard, and we support it. We are concerned by the direction of travel: the standalone bill introduced July 23 as H.R. 9925, which carries this draft's frontier provisions, shortens the window to 72 hours. That is the New York standard, not the California one. Seventy-two hours turns a federal report into a legal scramble and produces thin, lawyer-reviewed filings instead of useful technical detail. Keep 15 days.

**Protect the reports.** Incident reports will describe weight-security posture, incident response and other information that is a roadmap for adversaries. California exempts these submissions from its public records act. The federal text should say plainly that reports and related materials are confidential, exempt from disclosure under the Freedom of Information Act and protected from use in civil discovery except in enforcement actions.

**Add a safe harbor.** Pair the reporting duty with a good-faith safe harbor for developers that report promptly and reasonably. A reporting regime that punishes the companies that come forward will produce the silence it is meant to prevent.

We also ask you to hold the revenue line. The frontier developer tier begins at $50 million in gross revenue, and reporting duties attach there. Our data show what that means for a mid-size company: a $310,000 median one-time cost just to stand up the function. Please do not let this obligation drift down-market in response to pressure to widen coverage.

## 4. Section 112 independent verification: right idea, unfinished liability design

We support the tiering in the draft. The framework and audit duties attach to large frontier developers above $500 million in revenue, not to the $50 million tier. That concentration is the right instinct.

Section 112 still needs work before it becomes law. Please address four points. First, allocate liability clearly, so that a defective audit by a licensed verification organization does not become the developer's legal problem. Second, write conflict-of-interest and licensing rules that expand the pool of qualified auditors rather than concentrate audits in a handful of firms; a licensing bottleneck is a de facto release gate. Third, provide a real transition period, at least a full audit cycle, before the first semi-annual assessment, given that audits cannot begin until the framework, the licensees and the guidance all exist. Fourth, protect trade secrets and security-sensitive material in audit reports that go to CAISI and to enforcement authorities.

Finally, on penalties: liability of up to $1 million per day, enforceable by the attorney general and state attorneys general, is not light-touch. Please add notice and an opportunity to cure before penalties begin to accrue.

## 5. Section 102 CAISI: keep it voluntary

ACIA supports codifying the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at Commerce and supports its mandate to develop voluntary guidelines, best practices and standards. That is exactly the role a standards body should play, and our members already work with CAISI on a voluntary basis.

Our line is simple: standards yes, mandates no. We oppose any authority in Section 102 that would make pre-deployment government testing a condition of release, or that would require developers to hand over models or evaluations before deployment. Voluntary partnerships deliver the technical information CAISI needs without creating a federal approval step that no statute can keep pace with.

We take no position on the $100 million annual authorization; that is for the appropriators. We do note that the draft adds fee authority over verification organizations and large frontier developers. A fee on the regulated party is a compliance cost, and it should be bounded and reported.

## 6. What we support without reservation

The draft gets much right, and we want the record to reflect it. We support the GAO review of regulatory impediments to AI innovation in Section 122, the AI testbed work at the national labs and NIST, codification of the National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource, the CISA grants for maintainers of critical open-source packages, the GAO review of model-weight security, and the whistleblower protections in Section 113. We support the international standards provisions, including the exclusion of Chinese participation in U.S.-led standards coalitions. These are competitiveness provisions, and they deserve to move.

## 7. A closing note on how this bill talks about risk

The draft's instinct is correct: focus federal obligations on the largest developers, on demonstrated harms and on measurable capabilities. We urge you to hold that line as the text moves. Proposals will come from every direction, and many will be keyed to hypothetical catastrophic scenarios that cannot be defined, measured or litigated. Speculative risks are not a sound basis for legislation. Every dollar and every engineer-hour spent chasing a hypothetical is a dollar and an hour not spent on the compute buildout, the energy interconnection queues and the workforce that will actually determine whether the United States beats its competitors.

One national standard, light-touch and risk-based, applied to the biggest developers, and durable enough to plan against. That is what our members need from this bill, and it is what we are ready to help you write.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment. Our staff is available to work through any of these sections with your teams.

Respectfully,

Grant Holloway
President & CEO
American Compute & Innovation Alliance

function.arguments:
{"content": "# Internal fact-check and source notes for the GAAIA package (ACIA-POL-2026-117)

Not for external distribution. Prepared for Tessa Marchetti, VP Policy, and for the President & CEO's sign-off packet. Every factual claim in the package was checked against a primary or near-primary source on Oct. 16-17, 2026.

## Two corrections to our 2 Oct 2026 staff summary

1. **"Not yet formally introduced" is now out of date.** On July 23, 2026, Reps. Obernolte and Trahan introduced the FRONTIER Act, H.R. 9925, described by the sponsors as "developed as part of the broader Great American AI Act framework." It carries the discussion draft's frontier provisions. Referred to Energy and Commerce and to Science, Space, and Technology. The broader GAAIA package remains a discussion draft, and the sponsors are still collecting feedback at GAAIA@mail.house.gov, so the work order's channel is still valid.
2. **Section numbers are confirmed** (the summary carried a TODO). The comment letter cites them.

## Section numbers used in the package

From the sponsors' section-by-section summary (obernolte.house.gov, trahan.house.gov) and the draft text: Sec. 101 definitions; Sec. 102 CAISI; Sec. 111 transparency in frontier AI (frontier AI framework, transparency reports, incident reporting); Sec. 112 independent verification organizations; Sec. 113 whistleblower protections; Sec. 121 federalization/preemption of state development laws; Sec. 122 GAO report on regulatory impediments; Sec. 141 free-speech study.

## Key facts and where they were verified

- **Draft released June 4, 2026**, 269 pages, by Reps. Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.) and Lori Trahan (D-Mass.), with Franklin, Houchin, Peters and Subramanyam. Sponsors' press releases.
- **Preemption (Sec. 121):** three years; covers state laws "specifically regulating the development" of AI models; preserves state law on use/deployment, laws of general applicability and common-law remedies. DLA Piper analysis, Roll Call, Inside AI Policy (Oct. 15, 2026) and the draft text.
- **Critical safety incident (Sec. 101(7)):** (A) unauthorized access to, modification of, or exfiltration of model weights; (B) "a failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures"; (C) loss of control. No harm element. Draft text (trahan.house.gov, ari.us mirror).
- **Reporting clock in the draft:** 15 days to the CAISI director, 24 hours to law enforcement for imminent risk of death or serious physical injury. ArentFox Schiff client alert and the AI/TLDR summary of the draft.
- **H.R. 9925 moved to 72 hours** ("not later than 72 hours after a frontier developer learns facts sufficient to establish a reasonable belief that a critical safety incident has occurred"), plus a 24-hour imminent-risk trigger. Bill text at congress.gov and govinfo.gov.
- **California SB 53 comparison:** weight exfiltration and loss of control are reportable only where they "result[] in death or bodily injury"; 15-day reporting to Cal OES; reports exempt from the California Public Records Act. Business and Professions Code 22757.11 and 22757.13, leginfo.legislature.ca.gov.
- **New York RAISE:** chapter amendment signed March 27, 2026; effective Jan. 1, 2027; 72-hour reporting with a 24-hour imminent-risk trigger. Governor Hochul press releases, Wiley client alert.
- **Illinois SB 315:** signed July 6, 2026; effective Jan. 1, 2028; the only one of the three state laws requiring third-party audits. Illinois General Assembly status page, Gov. Pritzker release, Latham and Watkins and Morrison Foerster alerts.
- **Penalties in the draft:** up to $1 million per day; enforcement by the attorney general and, in certain circumstances, state attorneys general. Roll Call, Future of Privacy Forum.
- **IVOs (Sec. 112):** CAISI-licensed, retained by large frontier developers, semi-annual audits plus ad hoc audits at the CAISI director's request, access to unredacted materials, post-audit reports to CAISI, mandatory referral to the AG for imminent catastrophic risk. ArentFox Schiff and DLA Piper alerts.
- **Tiers:** frontier developer, more than $50 million in gross revenue with affiliates; large frontier developer, more than $500 million; frontier model, more than 10^26 operations. Framework and audit duties sit at the $500 million tier, transparency reports and incident reporting at the $50 million tier. ArentFox Schiff and Future of Privacy Forum.
- **CAISI (Sec. 102):** codified at Commerce; voluntary guidelines, best practices and standards; evaluates AI systems and monitors progress; synthetic content detection; administers IVO licensing; $100 million a year for FY2027-2029, plus fee authority over IVOs and large frontier developers. Sponsors' section-by-section and FAQ (the FAQ notes the current appropriation is about $15 million).
- **State AI law volume:** 36 states have enacted about 150 AI laws in 2026, per a 50-state tracker as of Oct. 15, 2026. Cited in the letter as "roughly 150 AI laws this year alone, across 36 states."
- **Administration policy:** Dec. 11, 2025 executive order "Ensuring a National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence" (AI Litigation Task Force, Commerce review of state laws); March 20, 2026 White House National Policy Framework for AI legislative recommendations, which asks Congress to preempt state AI laws that impose undue burdens and to bar states from regulating AI development. Federal Register, whitehouse.gov, Gibson Dunn and Jones Day summaries.
- **Current status (as of Oct. 15, 2026):** Energy and Commerce Chairman Brett Guthrie has not committed to a markup; Rep. Obernolte has said he wants a November committee vote; Rep. Ted Lieu has called for a markup; Rep. Trahan says the bill is "well-positioned to move." The Record, Blue Light News, State House News Service.

## Survey figures (from briefing/member_cost_survey_2026.md)

Used only in aggregate, per policy: 61% cite conflicting state definitions; median 6.5 FTEs for SB 53 plus RAISE; 34% of startups delayed a launch; $310,000 median one-time cost for incident reporting; $1.4 million median annual cost of a published frontier safety framework. The letter discloses the sample (86 responding members) and that it is self-reported. No member company is named anywhere in the package.

## Items deliberately not claimed

- We do not assert that the draft lacks any confidentiality provision for incident reports; we ask for confidentiality and a FOIA exemption without characterizing the current text.
- We do not assert the draft has no cure period; we ask for notice and an opportunity to cure.
- We take no position on the CAISI funding level, per the board-approved messaging guide.

## Open items for the requester

- Letter date is set at Oct. 29, 2026, in the following week's transmission window. Confirm the send date and add the alliance's street address to the letterhead.
- Confirm whether the CEO wants a separate transmittal email to GAAIA@mail.house.gov and whether we should copy committee staff.
- The letter references H.R. 9925's 72-hour clock. If you would rather not engage the introduced bill by name, delete that sentence; the 15-day ask stands on its own.

Fact-check flag before I finalize the GAAIA package (ACIA-POL-2026-117). Two things I verified online that differ from our 2 Oct staff summary, and one question on framing:

1. Section numbers are now confirmed: Sec. 101 (definitions), 102 (CAISI), 111 (frontier transparency + incident reporting), 112 (IVOs), 113 (whistleblowers), 121 (three-year preemption of state development laws), 122 (GAO report). I will cite these in the letter.

2. Our summary says the draft is "not yet formally introduced." On 23 July 2026 Obernolte and Trahan introduced the FRONTIER Act, H.R. 9925 (referred to E&C and Science), which is the standalone successor to GAAIA Title I. Notably, H.R. 9925 moved the critical-safety-incident reporting window from 15 days (as in the discussion draft, matching SB 53) to 72 hours with a 24-hour imminent-risk trigger, i.e., the RAISE Act standard our messaging guide opposes. It also adds a new Under Secretary of Commerce for AI Security and an AI-development-expenditure tier.

Question: do you want the letter framed purely as comments on the GAAIA discussion draft (and sent to GAAIA@mail.house.gov), or should it also engage H.R. 9925 by name? My default is to comment on the discussion draft and use H.R. 9925 as evidence that the reporting window is drifting from 15 days to 72 hours — that supports our ask to hold the SB 53 standard. Say the word if you want it framed otherwise; I'm proceeding on that default in the meantime.

|---|---|---|---|
| Sec. 121 - Preemption of state laws "specifically regulating the development" of AI models, with a three-year sunset | SUPPORT | Make the preemption permanent; at minimum extend it so a clean federal standard is enacted before any sunset date | A sunset that can revive SB 53 and RAISE in year four is a compliance cliff, so members never realize the cost relief. |
| Sec. 121 - Carve-outs preserving state law on use, deployment, general-applicability laws and common-law remedies | SUPPORT | Keep as drafted | A development standard should govern development, not strip state consumer, worker and fraud protections. |

| Sec. 102 - CAISI evaluation and testing of AI systems | OPPOSE ANY MANDATE | State expressly that pre-deployment testing and evaluation are voluntary and that no federal approval is required to deploy | Mandatory pre-deployment government testing is the heaviest possible hand and would function as a release gate. |

# DRAFT FOR PRESIDENT & CEO SIGN-OFF (due Fri 23 Oct 2026) - not for transmission

**AMERICAN COMPUTE & INNOVATION ALLIANCE**
Washington, D.C.

Oct. 29, 2026

Rep. Jay Obernolte
Rep. Lori Trahan
Committee on Energy and Commerce
U.S. House of Representatives
Washington, D.C. 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

**Re: Comments of the American Compute & Innovation Alliance on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft**

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

The American Compute & Innovation Alliance thanks you for releasing the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act as a discussion draft and for keeping the comment record open. ACIA is a Washington-based coalition of roughly 140 members: AI developers, cloud and data center operators, chip startups and venture firms. Our members build the models, chips and data centers that will determine whether the United States leads the world in artificial intelligence.

We write with one clear message. This draft is the first bipartisan text that would give the country one national standard for frontier AI development instead of a 50-state patchwork. That is the single most pro-innovation thing Congress can do this year. We support the architecture. We ask for five targeted changes as this text moves.

In our March 2025 comment to the Office of Science and Technology Policy on the AI Action Plan, ACIA urged the federal government to preempt the patchwork, unlock energy and compute, and keep standards voluntary and industry-led. The draft takes each of those ideas seriously, and we want to help you get it right.

## 1. The patchwork is the problem, and the costs are real

State legislatures have enacted roughly 150 AI laws this year alone, across 36 states. Three of them regulate frontier model development directly: California's SB 53, in effect since Jan. 1, 2026; New York's RAISE Act, as amended, effective Jan. 1, 2027; and Illinois' SB 315, signed July 6 and effective Jan. 1, 2028. They use different definitions, different reporting clocks and different audit rules. Illinois, unlike the other two, mandates third-party audits.

Our August 2026 member survey (86 responding members, self-reported, and cited here only in aggregate) quantifies what that means:

- Sixty-one percent of responding members cite conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem.
- Developers running SB 53 and RAISE in parallel report a median of 6.5 full-time employees devoted to compliance.
- Thirty-four percent of our startup members delayed a product launch in California or New York in the past 12 months because of state AI rules.
- Standing up an incident-reporting function costs a median of $310,000 before a company files a single report, and maintaining a published frontier safety framework costs larger developers a median of $1.4 million a year.

Compliance costs fall hardest on startups, even though these laws are written for the largest laboratories. That is backwards. The administration reached the same conclusion in its Dec. 11, 2025 executive order on a national AI policy framework and in the March 20, 2026 White House legislative recommendations, which ask Congress to preempt state laws that impose undue burdens and to keep states out of AI model development.

## 2. Section 121 preemption: we support it. Make it durable.

ACIA supports the draft's preemption of state laws that specifically regulate the development of AI models. The draft draws the right lines: state law on use, deployment and post-deployment harms is preserved, as are laws of general applicability and common-law remedies. Consumers, workers and state attorneys general keep their tools. What goes away is the duplication that comes from three states writing three different sets of pre-deployment rules for the same model.

Our ask is about duration, not scope. A three-year sunset is a compliance cliff. No compliance officer in our membership will dismantle a state-law program that may come back into force in year four, which means the cost relief the sponsors intend never materializes. We ask that Section 121 be made permanent. At minimum, extend it on a schedule that puts a clean, enacted federal standard in place before any sunset, with a Government Accountability Office review of the federal regime before the lapse date.

We also ask that preemption reach the specific development obligations the bill federalizes in Sections 111 and 112. A developer that complies with the federal standard should not also be answering to a state scheme covering the same conduct.

## 3. Section 111 incident reporting: we oppose it as drafted

ACIA does not oppose incident reporting. We oppose this version of it, and we ask for four changes.

**Narrow the definition.** Section 101(7) defines a critical safety incident to include "a failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures." Read literally, that captures every imperfect safeguard, with no harm shown. Compare California: under SB 53, unauthorized access to model weights is reportable when it "results in death or bodily injury," and loss of control likewise requires death or bodily injury. The draft strips those harm qualifiers out. It also drops the "single incident" limiter that California attaches to catastrophic risk. Please restore a harm or concrete-incident element, and keep federal obligations anchored to demonstrated harms rather than to speculative scenarios that no one can measure.

**Hold the 15-day clock.** The draft requires a report to the CAISI director within 15 days of discovery, which matches California, with a 24-hour disclosure to law enforcement where there is an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury. That is a workable, light-touch standard, and we support it. We are concerned by the direction of travel: the standalone bill introduced July 23 as H.R. 9925, which carries this draft's frontier provisions, shortens the window to 72 hours. That is the New York standard, not the California one. Seventy-two hours turns a federal report into a legal scramble and produces thin, lawyer-reviewed filings instead of useful technical detail. Keep 15 days.

**Protect the reports.** Incident reports will describe weight-security posture, incident response and other information that is a roadmap for adversaries. California exempts these submissions from its public records act. The federal text should say plainly that reports and related materials are confidential, exempt from disclosure under the Freedom of Information Act and protected from use in civil discovery except in enforcement actions.

**Add a safe harbor.** Pair the reporting duty with a good-faith safe harbor for developers that report promptly and reasonably. A reporting regime that punishes the companies that come forward will produce the silence it is meant to prevent.

We also ask you to hold the revenue line. The frontier developer tier begins at $50 million in gross revenue, and reporting duties attach there. Our data show what that means for a mid-size company: a $310,000 median one-time cost just to stand up the function. Please do not let this obligation drift down-market in response to pressure to widen coverage.

## 4. Section 112 independent verification: right idea, unfinished liability design

We support the tiering in the draft. The framework and audit duties attach to large frontier developers above $500 million in revenue, not to the $50 million tier. That concentration is the right instinct.

Section 112 still needs work before it becomes law. Please address four points. First, allocate liability clearly, so that a defective audit by a licensed verification organization does not become the developer's legal problem. Second, write conflict-of-interest and licensing rules that expand the pool of qualified auditors rather than concentrate audits in a handful of firms; a licensing bottleneck is a de facto release gate. Third, provide a real transition period, at least a full audit cycle, before the first semi-annual assessment, given that audits cannot begin until the framework, the licensees and the guidance all exist. Fourth, protect trade secrets and security-sensitive material in audit reports that go to CAISI and to enforcement authorities.

Finally, on penalties: liability of up to $1 million per day, enforceable by the attorney general and state attorneys general, is not light-touch. Please add notice and an opportunity to cure before penalties begin to accrue.

## 5. Section 102 CAISI: keep it voluntary

ACIA supports codifying the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at Commerce and supports its mandate to develop voluntary guidelines, best practices and standards. That is exactly the role a standards body should play, and our members already work with CAISI on a voluntary basis.

Our line is simple: standards yes, mandates no. We oppose any authority in Section 102 that would make pre-deployment government testing a condition of release, or that would require developers to hand over models or evaluations before deployment. Voluntary partnerships deliver the technical information CAISI needs without creating a federal approval step that no statute can keep pace with.

We take no position on the $100 million annual authorization; that is for the appropriators. We do note that the draft adds fee authority over verification organizations and large frontier developers. A fee on the regulated party is a compliance cost, and it should be bounded and reported.

## 6. What we support without reservation

The draft gets much right, and we want the record to reflect it. We support the GAO review of regulatory impediments to AI innovation in Section 122, the AI testbed work at the national labs and NIST, codification of the National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource, the CISA grants for maintainers of critical open-source packages, the GAO review of model-weight security, and the whistleblower protections in Section 113. We support the international standards provisions, including the exclusion of Chinese participation in U.S.-led standards coalitions. These are competitiveness provisions, and they deserve to move.

## 7. A closing note on how this bill talks about risk

The draft's instinct is correct: focus federal obligations on the largest developers, on demonstrated harms and on measurable capabilities. We urge you to hold that line as the text moves. Proposals will come from every direction, and many will be keyed to hypothetical catastrophic scenarios that cannot be defined, measured or litigated. Speculative risks are not a sound basis for legislation. Every dollar and every engineer-hour spent chasing a hypothetical is a dollar and an hour not spent on the compute buildout, the energy interconnection queues and the workforce that will actually determine whether the United States beats its competitors.

One national standard, light-touch and risk-based, applied to the biggest developers, and durable enough to plan against. That is what our members need from this bill, and it is what we are ready to help you write.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment. Our staff is available to work through any of these sections with your teams.

Respectfully,

Grant Holloway
President & CEO
American Compute & Innovation Alliance

# ONE PAGER: ACIA on the Great American AI Act discussion draft

**For Energy and Commerce offices - Oct. 2026 - American Compute & Innovation Alliance (140 members across AI development, cloud and data centers, semiconductors and venture capital)**

## One national standard beats 50 state regimes. Pass the preemption, fix the incident reporting.

ACIA supports the draft's architecture. It is the first bipartisan text that would replace a growing patchwork of state AI development laws with one national standard, and it concentrates obligations on the largest developers, not on startups. Three state frontier laws already stack up: California SB 53 (in force Jan. 1, 2026), New York RAISE (Jan. 1, 2027) and Illinois SB 315 (Jan. 1, 2028), each with different definitions, clocks and audit rules.

Our August 2026 member survey, in aggregate: 61% of members say conflicting state definitions are their top compliance problem; developers running SB 53 and RAISE together report a median 6.5 FTEs on compliance; 34% of our startup members delayed a California or New York launch in the past 12 months.

## Our asks

**1. Make the preemption durable (Sec. 121).**
We support preempting state laws that specifically regulate AI model development, and we support preserving state authority over use, deployment and general-applicability laws. A three-year sunset is a compliance cliff: nobody dismantles a state program that revives in year four. Make it permanent, or extend it with a clean federal standard enacted before any lapse.

**2. Narrow the critical safety incident definition (Sec. 101(7)).**
As drafted it covers "a failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures," with no harm shown. California requires death or bodily injury before model-weight exfiltration or loss of control is reportable. Restore a harm or concrete-incident element. Regulate demonstrated harms, not speculative scenarios.

**3. Hold the 15-day reporting clock (Sec. 111).**
The draft matches California's 15-day standard. The standalone bill carrying these provisions, H.R. 9925, moved to 72 hours, the New York standard. Keep 15 days, add confidentiality and a FOIA exemption, and add a good-faith safe harbor for reporters.

**4. Keep CAISI voluntary (Sec. 102).**
We support codifying CAISI and its voluntary standards role. We oppose any authority that turns pre-deployment government testing into a release gate. No position on the $100 million authorization; that is for appropriators.

**5. Fix the audit and penalty design (Sec. 112).**
Clarify liability for defective audits, license enough verifiers to avoid a bottleneck, allow a real transition period, and add notice and a chance to cure before million-dollar-per-day penalties.

**Bottom line:** one light-touch, risk-based national standard, applied to the biggest developers and durable enough to plan against. That keeps American AI investment here and compliance costs off startups.

Contact: ACIA policy team.

# Internal fact-check and source notes for the GAAIA package (ACIA-POL-2026-117)

Not for external distribution. Prepared for Tessa Marchetti, VP Policy, and for the President & CEO's sign-off packet. Every factual claim in the package was checked against a primary or near-primary source on Oct. 16-17, 2026.

## Two corrections to our 2 Oct 2026 staff summary

1. **"Not yet formally introduced" is now out of date.** On July 23, 2026, Reps. Obernolte and Trahan introduced the FRONTIER Act, H.R. 9925, described by the sponsors as "developed as part of the broader Great American AI Act framework." It carries the discussion draft's frontier provisions. Referred to Energy and Commerce and to Science, Space, and Technology. The broader GAAIA package remains a discussion draft, and the sponsors are still collecting feedback at GAAIA@mail.house.gov, so the work order's channel is still valid.
2. **Section numbers are confirmed** (the summary carried a TODO). The comment letter cites them.

## Section numbers used in the package

From the sponsors' section-by-section summary (obernolte.house.gov, trahan.house.gov) and the draft text: Sec. 101 definitions; Sec. 102 CAISI; Sec. 111 transparency in frontier AI (frontier AI framework, transparency reports, incident reporting); Sec. 112 independent verification organizations; Sec. 113 whistleblower protections; Sec. 121 federalization/preemption of state development laws; Sec. 122 GAO report on regulatory impediments; Sec. 141 free-speech study.

## Key facts and where they were verified

- **Draft released June 4, 2026**, 269 pages, by Reps. Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.) and Lori Trahan (D-Mass.), with Franklin, Houchin, Peters and Subramanyam. Sponsors' press releases.
- **Preemption (Sec. 121):** three years; covers state laws "specifically regulating the development" of AI models; preserves state law on use/deployment, laws of general applicability and common-law remedies. DLA Piper analysis, Roll Call, Inside AI Policy (Oct. 15, 2026) and the draft text.
- **Critical safety incident (Sec. 101(7)):** (A) unauthorized access to, modification of, or exfiltration of model weights; (B) "a failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures"; (C) loss of control. No harm element. Draft text (trahan.house.gov, ari.us mirror).
- **Reporting clock in the draft:** 15 days to the CAISI director, 24 hours to law enforcement for imminent risk of death or serious physical injury. ArentFox Schiff client alert and the AI/TLDR summary of the draft.
- **H.R. 9925 moved to 72 hours** ("not later than 72 hours after a frontier developer learns facts sufficient to establish a reasonable belief that a critical safety incident has occurred"), plus a 24-hour imminent-risk trigger. Bill text at congress.gov and govinfo.gov.
- **California SB 53 comparison:** weight exfiltration and loss of control are reportable only where they "result[] in death or bodily injury"; 15-day reporting to Cal OES; reports exempt from the California Public Records Act. Business and Professions Code 22757.11 and 22757.13, leginfo.legislature.ca.gov.
- **New York RAISE:** chapter amendment signed March 27, 2026; effective Jan. 1, 2027; 72-hour reporting with a 24-hour imminent-risk trigger. Governor Hochul press releases, Wiley client alert.
- **Illinois SB 315:** signed July 6, 2026; effective Jan. 1, 2028; the only one of the three state laws requiring third-party audits. Illinois General Assembly status page, Gov. Pritzker release, Latham and Watkins and Morrison Foerster alerts.
- **Penalties in the draft:** up to $1 million per day; enforcement by the attorney general and, in certain circumstances, state attorneys general. Roll Call, Future of Privacy Forum.
- **IVOs (Sec. 112):** CAISI-licensed, retained by large frontier developers, semi-annual audits plus ad hoc audits at the CAISI director's request, access to unredacted materials, post-audit reports to CAISI, mandatory referral to the AG for imminent catastrophic risk. ArentFox Schiff and DLA Piper alerts.
- **Tiers:** frontier developer, more than $50 million in gross revenue with affiliates; large frontier developer, more than $500 million; frontier model, more than 10^26 operations. Framework and audit duties sit at the $500 million tier, transparency reports and incident reporting at the $50 million tier. ArentFox Schiff and Future of Privacy Forum.
- **CAISI (Sec. 102):** codified at Commerce; voluntary guidelines, best practices and standards; evaluates AI systems and monitors progress; synthetic content detection; administers IVO licensing; $100 million a year for FY2027-2029, plus fee authority over IVOs and large frontier developers. Sponsors' section-by-section and FAQ (the FAQ notes the current appropriation is about $15 million).
- **State AI law volume:** 36 states have enacted about 150 AI laws in 2026, per a 50-state tracker as of Oct. 15, 2026. Cited in the letter as "roughly 150 AI laws this year alone, across 36 states."
- **Administration policy:** Dec. 11, 2025 executive order "Ensuring a National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence" (AI Litigation Task Force, Commerce review of state laws); March 20, 2026 White House National Policy Framework for AI legislative recommendations, which asks Congress to preempt state AI laws that impose undue burdens and to bar states from regulating AI development. Federal Register, whitehouse.gov, Gibson Dunn and Jones Day summaries.
- **Current status (as of Oct. 15, 2026):** Energy and Commerce Chairman Brett Guthrie has not committed to a markup; Rep. Obernolte has said he wants a November committee vote; Rep. Ted Lieu has called for a markup; Rep. Trahan says the bill is "well-positioned to move." The Record, Blue Light News, State House News Service.

## Survey figures (from briefing/member_cost_survey_2026.md)

Used only in aggregate, per policy: 61% cite conflicting state definitions; median 6.5 FTEs for SB 53 plus RAISE; 34% of startups delayed a launch; $310,000 median one-time cost for incident reporting; $1.4 million median annual cost of a published frontier safety framework. The letter discloses the sample (86 responding members) and that it is self-reported. No member company is named anywhere in the package.

## Items deliberately not claimed

- We do not assert that the draft lacks any confidentiality provision for incident reports; we ask for confidentiality and a FOIA exemption without characterizing the current text.
- We do not assert the draft has no cure period; we ask for notice and an opportunity to cure.
- We take no position on the CAISI funding level, per the board-approved messaging guide.

## Open items for the requester

- Letter date is set at Oct. 29, 2026, in the following week's transmission window. Confirm the send date and add the alliance's street address to the letterhead.
- Confirm whether the CEO wants a separate transmittal email to GAAIA@mail.house.gov and whether we should copy committee staff.

# Staff Q&A: anticipated questions on ACIA's GAAIA comments

Prepared for ACIA staff ahead of Hill meetings. Answers are capped at 120 words. Figures are from the August 2026 member compliance-cost survey, cited in aggregate only. Do not name member companies.

---

**1. Majority Energy and Commerce staff: "If you support preemption, why not support the incident-reporting provision? It's lighter than SB 53."**

Preemption answers where the rule comes from. Section 111 answers what the rule requires, and as drafted it is broader than SB 53, not lighter. Section 101(7) makes "a failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures" reportable with no harm shown. California requires death or bodily injury before weight exfiltration or loss of control counts as a critical safety incident. The draft also drops the "single incident" limiter the state laws use. The direction of travel is worse still: the standalone bill, H.R. 9925, moved the clock from 15 days to 72 hours. We will support a narrow reporting duty on the California standard, with confidentiality and a good-faith safe harbor. That is the fix we asked for.

---

**2. Minority staff, Trahan-aligned: "Your members say they take safety seriously. What federal safety obligations would you accept?"**

Plenty, and the draft already contains several we support: a published frontier AI framework and transparency reports at the $500 million tier, a narrow critical safety incident duty on the 15-day California clock, tiering by capability and revenue so obligations land on the largest developers, CAISI-led voluntary standards and voluntary testing partnerships, whistleblower protections, and GAO review of model-weight security. What we cannot accept is anything keyed to speculative catastrophic scenarios: mandatory pre-deployment government testing as a condition of release, or definitions that make every imperfect safeguard a reportable incident. Tie obligations to demonstrated harms and measurable capabilities. Our larger developers already publish frameworks voluntarily. The question is whether the federal version is workable enough to deliver one national standard.

---

**3. Senate Commerce staff: "Three years or permanent. What's the coalition's position on the preemption sunset?"**

Permanent. That is the board-approved position. Our letter asks that Section 121 preemption be made permanent, or extended so a clean federal standard is enacted before any sunset. Three years is a compliance cliff. No member will dismantle SB 53 and RAISE programs for a preemption that expires as they finish building them, so the cost relief never arrives. The stakes are concrete: 34% of our startup members delayed a California or New York launch in the past 12 months, and members report a median of 6.5 FTEs to run the two state regimes in parallel. If Congress insists on a three-year pilot, pair it with the Section 122 GAO report and an extension vote before the lapse.

---

**4. Appropriations staff: "CAISI is authorized at $100 million a year. What's your view on the funding level?"**

We do not have one. The board has taken no position on the dollar figure, and our comment letter says so. Our interest is the mission, not the appropriation: CAISI's standards and evaluation work should stay voluntary and industry-led, and the bill should not let the center make pre-deployment testing a condition of release. Two points for the subcommittee. First, the draft adds fee authority over verification organizations and large frontier developers, a new cost on the regulated party that should be bounded and reported. Second, CAISI is appropriated at roughly $15 million today, a large step up; members will want a staffing and workload plan for the out-years. We can supply aggregate cost data on request.
